Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the Authors)

In the introduction, it would be helpful if the authors mention the age range and functioning level of participants for every prior study they cite that used eye-tracking to assess social attention in autism. In addition, statements such as "these atypicalities are present early" should include what is meant by early (what age range).

35 age-matched TD children were used to obtain normative gaze patterns, but it is not clear how this number was determined. Are there either power analyses or previous data suggesting that this sample size is sufficient to determine what is normative? A related issue is that of age norms. How were age-specific norms considered, given that the sample include children between 2-7 years of age and was not very large (eg. it is not clear how many children of each age were included in the sample)?

In addition to child adaptive behavior, were any other assessments conducted and if so, were they related to visual exploration patterns in children? Were any of the visual exploration metrics related to severity of autism symptoms?

There is not much information provided regarding the TD sample. What screening tools and procedures were used to detect neurological or psychiatric diseases?

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the Authors)

The main novelty of the study lies in a longitudinal component. Some of the subjects were tested again, about a year apart. Using a sliding window approach, these data were used to derive continuous measures of gaze atypicality over age (this analysis was complemented by a more rigid analyses based only on those subjects with two datapoints one year apart). Median contour surface and convergence index were the two metrics used here. Both showed developmental differences between groups. Visual features in the video were examined using a saliency model, and social complexity was quantified as the number of characters on the screen while controlling for overall visual complexity. Overall, it was found that while spatial divergence in gaze decreased in the TD group (convergence index increased) over the developmental time window examined, this was not the case for the ASD group (Figure 3).

These are labor-intensive and valuable data that will certainly add to the literature on attention and visual processing in ASD. The longitudinal dataset is quite special, and the results are in broad strokes fairly compelling: there are different developmental trajectories in visual attention in ASD compared to TD controls. The methods are reasonably sophisticated (but see my comments below). My main hesitation with this study is that it stops short of providing a stronger mechanistic advance. In particular, the developmental eye tracking data are really the centerpiece of the work. However, they are not linked to any other developmental measures. Actually, it was unclear to me at which timepoints the other behavioral measures (Vineland, etc.) were measured. It would have been ideal to get the Vineland and other measures of functioning at each of the specific timepoints, one year apart, at which the eye tracking data were collected to examine associations. But that seems not do have been done (or at least is not reported).

A second shortcoming of the study is the lack of detail with respect to individual subjects (were there any clusters/subgroups/outliers of interest?) and with respect to stimulus features that could be driving the observed effects. There is the saliency analysis, and an analysis of how many characters are on the screen, but that is it. Surely one could quantify additional semantic features, even if ratings are obtained from adults. As it stands there are unconnected analyses in the study. For instance, I have the bottom of Figure 1, showing that proximity index in a subject with ASD varies tremendously over the frames of the movie. Does it vary like that in other subjects with ASD? Does this variation line up with specific features in the video? Most importantly, I would want to see the framewise plot like this (or better: slightly temporally smoothed) of proximity index differences between TD and ASD, as a function of the longitudinal data. What features in the video correlate with the increased convergence seen in TD that are missing in ASD? The analyses provided do not back out these specifics, and without them the story is more descriptive than mechanistic.

1. Since the TD group was always used as a reference, and single ASD participants were compared to this "norm", we do not have a good estimate of how TD subjects would look by comparison. A stronger approach would calculate the TD norm in a leave-one-out fashion and generate distributions for how each individual TD subject also compared – those are the data then to compare (single TD and single ASD) rather than just ASD individuals to one fixed TD average. The authors refer to their analyses as "data-driven", and it is perhaps that with respect to not using ROIs on the video, but they are testing specific differences between pre-defined groups (ASD and TD). It would substantially strengthen the paper if indeed a data-driven analyses were provided (clustering the subject groups on the basis of the data, rather than as predefined). This could also help reveal possible outliers (in both groups) as well as possible subgroups.

2. It is intriguing that the fixation durations between groups differed. I wonder if the authors would consider inspecting smooth pursuit, a type of oculomotor feature not mentioned but that could be relevant (and has been reported to be atypical in ASD).

3. Subjects: More information on the subjects is needed. On what criteria were ASD and TD matched, was level of functioning or intellect taken into consideration? Did ASD subjects have a DSM diagnosis? Was the ADI done? What exclusionary criteria were applied (epilepsy, comorbidity, medication, etc?). More info please.

4. Analysis: proximity index. Why was the proximity index not temporally smoothed? A frame-by-frame metric will (a) have relatively sparse normative distributions, and (b) show fairly discontinuous gaze proximity (as evident in the plot shown in Figure 1, bottom).

5. All of the analyses are within-sample and use standard parametric statistics; it would be preferable to use cross-validation together with permutation testing for a more robust approach. For correlations between gaze data and behavioral data, it seems that about 10 correlation analyses were done. It would be important to correct for the multiple tests. This is also a particularly problematic issue in the saliency analyses, where there are several that are barely at the magic "P<0.05" threshold.

6. Eyetracking exclusions. This is insufficiently described in the paper. We are only told that subjects were excluded if >45% of frames were dropped. First of all, this is an extremely lenient threshold. But we need to know what the distribution of dropped frames was between ASD and TD groups. We also need to know what other exclusions were applied to any portion of the data. Right now, only complete subject-wise exclusions are mentioned, but surely that was not the only criterion.

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the Authors)

These results are interesting and valuable to our understanding of the development of social visual attention. However, several weaknesses should be addressed that would strengthen the results. First, the authors assume Gaussian distribution of TD eye gaze, but some of their example figures show that this is not always the case. This may lead to lower proximity index scores and may inflate the significant results rather than reflecting the true proximity of gaze to the normative distribution. Second, it would be helpful to discuss more of the individual differences in normative viewing to help anchor some of the main points of the paper. Finally, causality is assumed in the lower-level visual saliency analyses when instead the social and visual saliency may be highly correlated (and inseparable).

It would be helpful if the authors could provide more details about the π scores, specifically the normalization of them. The authors should explain how the normalization of the π scores was conducted and if this normalization allows for consistency across frames, where the possible furthest distance from the mode of the Gaussian distribution may change depending on the x- and y-coordinates of the mode of the Gaussian on the screen. Additionally, a description of how the normalization of π scores may change based on the convergence of TD children (i.e., how peaked the distribution is) would be helpful. If and how these measures may be limited should be discussed. Additionally, Figure 1 shows a child's π score on a frame-by-frame level across the video. Frames where the child was looking offscreen were coded as -0.15. The authors should explain why this value was chosen, and why a value was chosen at all instead of excluding these frames from analysis. Additionally, it would be important to know that these frames are moments that the child is looking off-screen and not moments where the child is blinking.

It is unclear how the authors handled instances where there were two distinct clusters of gaze distribution and the distribution was therefore not Gaussian. This will directly impact the π score and may make children with ASD look more atypical in their viewing patterns than they truly are. For example, Figure 3b shows both groups having two distinct clusters of visual attention, but more children with ASD are attending to the second focal point than TD children. Additional information on these instances should be added, and limitations should be discussed.

It would be helpful if the authors could validate their normative gaze distribution with leave-one-out procedures or some other method to ensure that the normative distribution is not shifted by one participant. This same procedure would be necessary for the maturational sliding window to show that the gaze pattern is actually reflecting developmental change, not just change due to individual differences in two participants' gaze data (the participant newly included and the participant newly excluded in the sliding window).

It would be worthwhile to include a figure of the correlation of π and autism symptom severity in Figure 2.

In Figure 3c-d, what do the shaded regions represent?

Mean and standard errors of the Proximity Index were not reported for every comparison Figure 4. This could also be collapsed to a difference score for each participant to allow easier comparisons across figures. This particular analysis is complex and would benefit from some greater explanation of the comparisons and how to interpret them in both the results and the Discussion section. This feels like it would be the primary analysis of the paper and it was under-developed in both the results and discussion.

The authors could consider strengthening their results by including some additional analyses exploring individual differences. Children with ASD on the whole become less convergent with each other over time, but are there children who become more convergent with the TD group and those who do not?

A decent amount of space in the paper is dedicated to analyses that are only included in the supplemental analyses. The authors may consider restructuring some of the main and supplemental texts such that the relevant figures will appear near the analyses.

The authors suggest a direction of causality wherein TD children are relying more on lower-level salient features of the scene than are children with ASD. However, salient features of a scene as predicted by the Itti & Koch model are often highly correlated with the social aspects of a scene. Especially in a cartoon, backgrounds remain consistent and the only movement is vibrantly-colored characters moving across the scene. The authors should edit the methods to exclude the suggestion of causality and the above point should be discussed.

The authors should discuss why gaze behavior correlated with adaptive behavior scales but not with overall autism symptom severity.

In general, additional context could be provided to the Results section to clarify what questions the authors were trying to answer with each analysis.

As far as I understand, they calculated the group divergence from 20 resampled data to generate a 'null divergence' for each group, then calculate that difference 100 times as a null distribution of the group difference, and finally compare the actual group difference with this null distribution. However, from their response letter, the distribution seems to be the group-level dispersion, but not the group difference. In their rebuttal letter, the authors write, "We applied 100 permutations inside each of the 59 windows (containing 20TD + 20ASD gaze recordings) to derive a null distribution of the measure of dispersion -the average pairwise distance between gaze coordinates inside the group." This seems inconsistent.

– In the Method of the "Maturational changes in visual exploration of complex social scene – Sliding window approach", in the second paragraph, the authors mention a reference distribution. However, this reference distribution seems not to have been used in any of the analyses (it's not mentioned in the longitudinal results at all). To quote from the paper: "Upon the creation of sliding windows and to characterize the group's visual behavior and its change with age, gaze data from the TD group were pooled together to define the referent distribution in each of the 59 age windows. To characterize the group visual behavior in the ASD group, we performed the same by pooling the gaze data together from ASD in each of the 59 age windows (see Figure 8 A&B)." Indeed, Figure 8A is about how to decide the sliding window, and Figure 8B is about pairwise gaze dispersion, not about referent distribution.

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

The present research uses the Typical Development (TD) group as a normative reference, comparing individual participants with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) against this reference. However, as pointed out by Reviewer #2, this approach doesn't allow for a comprehensive understanding of the variation within the TD group itself. The leave-one-out calculation suggests that the π is higher for TD, but the TD group is also more homogenous, so I am not sure this is truly informative. A comparison between TD and ASD groups at the individual subject level could provide more insightful information.

Additional Concerns:

i) The study matches the two groups based on chronological age rather than mental age. This introduces a potential confound as the differences reported may be indicative of general developmental delays rather than ASD-specific characteristics.

ii) The TD group is not only smaller in size but also less heterogeneous, which may be a potential explanation for the findings illustrated in Figure 8C.

results.result: Children with ASD showed significantly divergent moment-to-moment gaze patterns compared to TD peers when viewing a social cartoon, as measured by the Proximity Index (PI). The study included 166 males with ASD (mean age 3.37±1.16 years) and 51 age-matched TD males (mean age 3.48±1.29 years), with a statistically significant difference in average PI values between groups (t(215)=5.51, p<0.001).
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C44, and C43 provide converging evidence for divergent gaze patterns in ASD. The statistical analysis (C44) demonstrates a significant group difference with appropriate sample sizes (C43), and the finding is clearly stated as a primary result (C2). The t-test is appropriate for comparing means between two independent groups, and the p-value indicates strong statistical significance.

results.result: Higher PI values (indicating more TD-like gaze patterns) in children with ASD were associated with better developmental functioning across all six PEP-3 domains and better adaptive functioning across all four VABS-II domains. The PLS-C analysis yielded one significant latent component (r=0.331, p=0.001), with the strongest loadings on verbal/preverbal cognition and fine motor skills among developmental measures.
results.evaluation: Claims C45, C46, C98, C111, and C63 collectively demonstrate a robust relationship between gaze patterns and functional outcomes. The PLS-C multivariate approach is appropriate for handling correlated behavioral measures, the statistical significance is clearly reported (C98), and the pattern is stable across multiple domains. The interpretation regarding fine motor skills (C111) is reasonable given the attentional component of this measure.

results.result: Children with ASD showed significantly more ambient fixations (U=2530, p<0.001) and fewer focal fixations (U=2345, p<0.001) compared to TD children, though focal fixations were more frequent than ambient in both groups. Higher focal fixation proportion positively correlated with PI in both groups (rTD=0.459, rASD=0.434, p<0.001), while ambient fixations showed the opposite pattern (rTD=−0.400, rASD=−0.31, p=0.002). This suggests ASD children spent more time in ambient exploration mode and less in focused attention mode.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C51 provide strong statistical evidence for differences in fixation patterns, with appropriate non-parametric tests (Mann-Whitney U) and correlation analyses. Claims C71, C114-C116 offer reasonable interpretations linking these patterns to attentional modes, supported by citation to prior work (C72). The correlations between fixation types and PI provide convergent validity for the PI measure.

results.result: Contrary to the hypothesis, the GBVS salience model better predicted gaze allocation in TD children compared to ASD children across all channels (intensity, orientation, color, flicker, motion) and the full model (p<0.001 for all comparisons). This indicates that basic visual properties of the scene played a less important role in directing gaze in ASD children compared to TD peers.
results.evaluation: Claims C52, C64, C75, and C5 consistently report this unexpected finding with appropriate statistical testing (Wilcoxon test). The result contradicts the initial hypothesis but is clearly stated and statistically significant. However, the authors acknowledge potential confounds related to the young age of the sample (C117) and note that salience models may be better suited for mature visual systems (C77). The finding is robust but interpretation requires caution.

results.result: Among video content features, social complexity had the strongest impact on gaze divergence in ASD children. Lower PI (greater divergence from TD patterns) was associated with higher social complexity (multiple characters), higher visual complexity, and directed speech. Conversely, monologue, frame changes, and moving background increased PI. The PLS-C analysis yielded one significant latent component (r=0.331, p<0.001).
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C58 and C100 provide statistical evidence from PLS-C analysis, which is appropriate given the collinearity among predictors. Claims C3, C65, and C66 interpret these findings in terms of social interaction processing difficulties. The pattern is coherent and statistically significant, though the interpretation regarding social interaction difficulties (C66) involves some inference beyond the data. The use of PLS-C is well-justified given the high correlation between visual and social complexity (r=0.763).

results.result: In longitudinal analysis (n=81 ASD children with complete data at both timepoints), lower PI values at T1 predicted higher autism symptom severity at T2 (one year later), with one significant latent component (r=0.287, p=0.033). However, PI at T1 was not related to cognition or adaptation at T2.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C60, C101, C103, and C69 provide evidence for predictive validity of the PI measure for symptom trajectory. The PLS-C analysis is appropriate for this longitudinal design, and the statistical significance is clearly reported. The lack of relationship with cognition and adaptation at T2 (C60) is also clearly stated. However, the authors acknowledge potential explanations for why the relationship was not significant at T1 (C120, C123), including symptom instability and TD gaze maturation, which adds appropriate nuance to the interpretation.

results.result: Using a sliding window approach with 59 age-matched windows spanning ages 1.88-4.28 years, TD children showed progressively convergent gaze patterns (decreasing dispersion) with age, while ASD children showed the opposite pattern with increasing dispersion. Statistically significant differences in gaze dispersion between groups were observed in 46 consecutive windows starting at age 2.5-4.3 years. This pattern remained robust when controlling for sample size and developmental age.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C62, C67-C68, C6, C79-C80, and C104-C106 provide comprehensive evidence for divergent developmental trajectories using an appropriate sliding window approach. The permutation testing (C105) provides valid statistical inference, and the robustness analyses (C106) address potential confounds. The finding is consistent with prior cross-sectional work (C81) but extends it with longitudinal data. The methodological approach is sound, though the authors acknowledge limitations related to TD sample size (C93).

results.result: At T2 (mean age 4.05±0.929 years), simultaneous PLS-C analysis showed that higher PI coexisted with lower autistic symptoms and higher adaptive behavior scores (r=0.322, p=0.014). The relationship between PI and autism symptoms was significant at T2 but not at the younger T1 timepoint (mean age 3.01±0.885 years).
results.evaluation: Claims C102 and C103 report a significant cross-sectional relationship at T2 with appropriate statistical methods. The lack of significant relationship at T1 is acknowledged, and the authors provide plausible explanations including symptom instability in younger children (C120-C122) and maturation of TD gaze patterns providing a more sensitive reference at T2 (C123-C124). The interpretation is appropriately cautious.

results.result: The authors conclude that social attention should be targeted early in clinical treatments for ASD, based on findings of progressive divergence in gaze patterns during childhood and the predictive value of early gaze patterns for later symptom severity. They propose the PI method as a promising tool for understanding developmental mechanisms in ASD.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C91, and C92 represent clinical and methodological implications drawn from the empirical findings. While these are recommendations rather than direct empirical results, they are logically supported by the data showing (1) progressive divergence with age, (2) predictive validity for symptom trajectory, and (3) associations with functional outcomes. However, these remain recommendations for future work rather than demonstrated interventions.

results.result: Screen attendance was significantly higher in TD children (93.8±6.37s) compared to ASD children (87.8±9.33s), U=2568, p<0.001. There was a non-significant trend for longer median fixation duration in TD children compared to ASD (t(215)=1.85, p=0.06).
results.evaluation: Claims C96 and C97 report basic group differences in eye-tracking metrics with appropriate statistical tests. The significant difference in screen attendance (C96) is a potential confound that the authors address by excluding non-fixation data in calculations. The trend-level difference in fixation duration (C97) is appropriately reported as non-significant but suggestive.

results.result: The Proximity Index (PI) was calculated using adaptive kernel density estimation on TD gaze data for each frame, with lower PI values indicating greater divergence from the TD reference. Bootstrap stability analyses indicated that the TD sample size of 51 was sufficient, being more than twice the estimated minimum stable sample size of 18.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C110 describe the methodological approach for calculating the PI measure. The use of adaptive kernel density estimation (C108) is appropriate for handling variable gaze distributions across frames. The bootstrap stability analysis (C110) provides important validation that the reference sample size is adequate. The method is clearly described and statistically sound.

results.result: The authors acknowledge that the lack of a TD control group of comparable size to the ASD group was a severe limitation. They propose that the PI method can be applied to any eye-tracking paradigm and has potential for population-wide developmental studies and automated ASD screening.
results.evaluation: Claim C93 appropriately identifies a significant limitation that affects statistical power and precision of the TD reference. Claims C94 and C95 propose future applications of the method, but these remain speculative (as indicated by evidence_type SPECULATION and INFERENCE). The generalizability and screening utility of the method require empirical validation in independent samples and different contexts.

results.result: In previous work by the authors on a smaller sample with simultaneous EEG recording, divergence in gaze deployment was associated with abnormalities in neural activation, including reduced frontal/cingulate activation and increased inferior parietal/temporal/cerebellar activation. Children with less divergent (more TD-like) gaze patterns showed greater engagement of median cingulate cortex and paracentral regions, suggesting potential compensatory strategies.
results.evaluation: Claims C73 and C74 reference findings from prior work (Jan et al., 2019) rather than presenting new results from the current study. While C73 reports empirical findings from that prior work, C74 involves speculation about compensatory mechanisms (evidence_type includes SPECULATION). These claims provide context but are not direct results of the current manuscript. The compensatory interpretation requires further validation.

results.result: The fine motor scale of the PEP-3, in addition to measuring hand/wrist muscle control, also reflects the child's capacity to stay focused during controlled actions. This attentional component may explain the high loading of fine motor skills in the latent component pattern relating PI to developmental functioning.
results.evaluation: Claims C112 and C113 provide a reasonable interpretation of why fine motor skills showed strong association with PI. Claim C112 describes an established property of the PEP-3 fine motor scale (evidence_type KNOWLEDGE), while C113 offers a plausible mechanistic interpretation (evidence_type INFERENCE). The interpretation is logical given that scene viewing requires eye movement control, though it remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: The authors suggest that the relatively young age of their sample and potential visual/motor abnormalities in this age range might have influenced the lesser success of salience models in predicting gaze allocation in ASD children.
results.evaluation: Claim C117 offers a speculative explanation for the unexpected salience model findings, supported by citations to prior work. However, this remains a post-hoc interpretation without direct empirical support from the current data. The explanation is plausible but would require additional analyses or data to confirm, such as age-stratified analyses or direct assessment of visual/motor abilities.

results.result: Social interaction processing depends strongly on top-down inputs including prior expectations, attributed meaning, and language/scene understanding. ASD children with greater deficits in these top-down processing skills showed lower (less TD-like) PI values.
results.evaluation: Claim C118 states established knowledge about social interaction processing (evidence_type KNOWLEDGE), while C119 interprets the PLS-C results in this framework (evidence_type DATA and INFERENCE). The interpretation is reasonable given the strong association between PI and social complexity (C53) and the involvement of verbal/preverbal cognition in the behavioral pattern (C111). However, the inference about top-down processing deficits is indirect.

results.result: The authors propose two possible explanations for the lack of stable association between PI and autistic symptoms at T1: (1) lower stability of ASD symptoms in younger children, with diagnosis fluctuations more likely in children with milder symptoms, and (2) maturation of TD gaze patterns resulting in a tighter, more sensitive reference distribution at T2.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C125 present speculative interpretations (evidence_type includes SPECULATION) of the null finding at T1. While both explanations are plausible and supported by citations to prior work (C122), they remain post-hoc interpretations without direct empirical support from the current data. The authors appropriately present these as possible interpretations rather than definitive explanations. Additional analyses or data would be needed to distinguish between these alternatives.

results.result: The authors note that early intensive behavioral intervention improves symptoms and functioning in ASD, and suggest that future research should examine how gaze behavior is influenced by intervention and how behavioral profiles change following changes in visual behavior.
results.evaluation: Claim C126 states established knowledge about intervention efficacy (evidence_type KNOWLEDGE), while C127 proposes future research directions (evidence_type SPECULATION). These are appropriate recommendations based on the study findings, but they represent suggestions for future work rather than empirical results from the current study.
